rationale_and_sources: Surplus is remunerated through net settlement and the supplier/BRP chain, and settlement is routine. Multiple independent retail routes were not found [47–50].

The electricity and renewable-energy acts and BEK 1069/2021 implement REC and CEC definitions, rights, obligations and enabling rules. Danish Energy Agency grants support projects run by established energy communities, but no register or activity statistics were found [18,47–49,91].

Collective self-consumption operates behind a single main meter with sub-meters and one shared supplier. Sharing over the public grid was not possible at the cutoff, as Energinet’s sharing platform was still under development [49,50,52,53].
P2P rights exist, as do bilateral and aggregator-mediated analogues. A standard decentralised settlement market between customers was not found [47–51].
Local exchanges remain subject to ordinary network tariffs. No general locational relief was found in operation [51].
Mature, non-discriminatory routes to wholesale and flexibility markets run through suppliers, aggregators and BRPs [47,50].

Energinet prequalifies aggregated portfolios, demand facilities included, for FCR, FCR-N/D, FFR, aFRR and mFRR. In DK2 the minimum bid for frequency-containment and fast-frequency products is 0.1–0.3 MW, and elsewhere it is 1 MW. FCR (DK1), FFR and FCR-D (DK2) can be offered without a BRP contract. In all other cases imbalance responsibility is delegated through established BRP arrangements [50,99,100].

Under flex or quarter-hour settlement, metering points are settled on 15-minute values. Grid companies send metered data to DataHub every day. DataHub validates the data and forwards them to suppliers by 08:00 the next day [50,101].
Injection is metered separately and paid for under supplier contracts based on quarter-hourly data [54–56].

The region has implemented the REC/CEC framework, registration and permitted activities, and 80 energy communities were registered by September 2025. Federal competence still applies to transmission and balancing [18,54,55,57].
Fluvius runs energy sharing, with defined allocation rules and quarter-hourly settlement [55,56].
Energy selling is expressly allowed and works through the DSO data process. Settlement is still organised around suppliers [55,56].
Sharing lowers only the energy component of the bill. Network tariffs, levies and administrative costs apply in full to shared energy, with no specific tariff treatment [55,56].
Prosumers reach energy and flexibility markets through suppliers and aggregators, and both routes are in use [54,55].

Balancing is regulated at Belgian level. Elia admits aggregated portfolios, low-voltage units included, as balancing service providers. About 17,000 low-voltage delivery points take part in FCR, and aFRR has been open to low-voltage units since 2024. Transfer-of-energy, opt-out and pass-through arrangements allow a BSP to operate independently of the supplier and its BRP. No community-specific route was identified. Low-voltage participation is so far limited to FCR, with no aFRR volume yet and mFRR access planned for 2026, so L4 is not awarded [58,59].
Sharing and energy selling rely on digital meters and validated quarter-hourly data [56].
Exported and shared renewable electricity is paid for through GSE mechanisms that are in operation [60–63].
Legislative Decree 199/2021 and its implementing acts have put the CER framework, registration, governance rules and national incentives into operation [60–63].
Virtual sharing works under ARERA rules and GSE procedures, with shared energy calculated hourly [61–63]. This interval is longer than the 15-minute Italian imbalance settlement period [87].
No explicit legal status for P2P sale was found. PPAs, market sales and CER allocation act as functional analogues [60–63].

Shared energy earns an incentive and, under the TIAD, a partial restitution of network-tariff components calculated on hourly shared energy. Otherwise, network charges follow the standard tariffs, with no general use-based local tariff [61,62].
Producers and communities can sell through GSE, the market, PPAs or aggregators. Access runs through licensed parties and is in operation [60–63].

Aggregated mixed units (UVAM), which may combine small generation, storage and demand, are enabled to provide dispatching services to the TSO. The regime has operated since the 2018 pilot and is now part of the TIDE. No community-specific pathway was found [60,61,64,87].
Hourly metering, virtual allocation and GSE settlement are in place and working [61–63].

Net billing and related surplus-settlement models were defined by the 2024 ministerial decision, and HEDNO connects net-billing units. Crediting of exported energy was often delayed by missing DAPEEP and HEDNO data, and the revised framework was adopted only after the cutoff [65,66,72].
REC, CEC and older energy-community forms all have a legal basis, and many projects are documented [18,73,74].
Metering and allocation procedures are defined for virtual net billing and collective arrangements, and the operational rules are in force [72–74].
There is a right to sell, and bilateral contracts serve as analogues. An explicit P2P settlement mechanism in operation was not found [73,74].
Normal tariffs, charges and taxes still apply, and no general tariff relief for local sharing is in operation [72].

Renewable stations, community-owned ones included, sell through licensed aggregators or through the last-resort aggregator run by DAPEEP. This route works. Direct access of communities to flexibility markets is not documented [67,72–74].

Demand-response aggregators register as balancing service providers through IPTO’s Dispatchable Load Registry, and aggregated loads have provided mFRR since 2023. A balancing pathway specific to communities is not defined [68,69].

Fifteen-minute settlement provisions and DSO metering rules exist. The smart-meter rollout was under way but incomplete at the cutoff, with national coverage planned by 2030, so most low-voltage sharing was still settled without validated interval data [70–72].
According to DGEG, unconsumed surplus may be sold to the grid. Decree-Law 15/2022 sets up market, aggregator and bilateral routes, all of which operate [75,76].
Decree-Law 15/2022 sets out REC and CEC entities, proximity conditions and system roles. According to the Government, 1,218 energy communities were connected to the grid in April 2026 [18,75,96].
Collective self-consumption and energy sharing are run by an internal manager, with the DSO calculating allocations from 15-minute coefficients [75,77].
The law recognises P2P commercialisation. No decentralised settlement market between customers was found in routine use [75,77].

Self-consumed energy carried over the public grid pays dedicated ERSE network-access tariffs, covering only the voltage levels used. The separate reduction of CIEG components relieves policy costs and is not a network-cost criterion [75,77].
Surplus can be sold through aggregators, markets or bilateral contracts, with licensed parties operating the route [75–77].

Consumption units may provide mFRR under the system-management rules approved by ERSE in 2023. Participation through aggregation of small units and a transparent imbalance allocation for communities were not documented [75–77,79].
Fifteen-minute allocation coefficients, DSO calculation and electronic procedures make settlement operational [75–77].
Under the Clean Export Guarantee, exported electricity must be paid for and suppliers execute these payments [83–85].
There are rules for REC recognition and support schemes and CRU recognises community activities. The statutory REC/CEC route is still incomplete [18,84–86].
Energy sharing is recognised as a community activity. By the cutoff, however, no routine process for multi-party allocation and settlement had been documented [84,86].
No explicit P2P status was found, and supplier export contracts are the only functional analogue [84,86].
The review identified no special network-charge treatment for shared or locally traded electricity [83,84].
Demand side units aggregate individual demand sites and are registered in the single electricity market. Suppliers and the renewable support scheme provide further routes to the market [80,81,83–86].
Demand side units are scheduled and dispatched in the balancing market. A route for communities to delegate imbalance responsibility was not found [80,81,84,86].

More than two million smart meters (over four in five households) are installed, and the exports of over 140,000 smart-meter customers are paid on metered data. Data processes for multi-party sharing are still being developed [82–85].
